data.title: NVIDIA vs. AMD: Data-Center Risk Factors and Margins (Last 2 Fiscal Years)

report.title: NVIDIA vs. AMD: Data-Center Risk Factors and Margins (Last 2 Fiscal Years)
report.summary: NVIDIA’s margins remain far higher than AMD’s, but NVIDIA’s gross margin declined in FY2026 amid the transition to Blackwell systems and a sizable inventory charge, while AMD’s margins improved in FY2025 on mix despite export-control-related charges. NVIDIA highlights risks from export controls, China-specific standards, long lead times, non‑cancellable commitments, and dependence on Asian supply, whereas AMD emphasizes AI-demand uncertainty, customers’ power/water constraints for data centers, climate-related disruptions, and rapid product transitions (plus competitive pressure from NVIDIA). For research and education only; not investment advice.

sections.heading: Margins: Last 2 Fiscal Years (side by side)

claims.text: NVIDIA margins remained very high but edged lower year over year: gross margin 75.0% (FY2025) to 71.1% (FY2026); operating margin 62.4% to 60.4%; net margin 55.9% to 55.6%.

NVIDIA attributed the FY2026 gross margin decline to shifting from Hopper HGX to Blackwell full‑scale datacenter solutions and a $4.5 billion H20 excess inventory and purchase‑obligation charge; in FY2025, gross margin benefited from a higher Data Center revenue mix despite inventory-related headwinds.
AMD’s margins improved year over year: gross margin 49.4% (FY2024) to 49.5% (FY2025); operating margin 7.4% to 10.7%; net margin 6.4% to 12.5%.

AMD noted that FY2025 gross margin rose on product mix but was partially offset by approximately $440 million of net inventory and related charges tied to U.S. export controls on Instinct MI308; in FY2024, margin improved on mix as Data Center and Client grew.

Long manufacturing lead times, uncertain supply and capacity availability, and reliance on non‑cancellable orders create mismatch risks between supply and demand; complex data center buildouts can be impeded by third‑party component shortages.

Export controls on AI GPUs can restrict use, resale, repair or transfer of products and disrupt NVIDIA’s supply chain and cloud/services offerings globally, potentially benefiting competitors less likely to be restricted.

China-specific policies pose added risk: new accelerator efficiency standards and other government actions (e.g., restrictions tied to suppliers like Micron) could limit customers’ use of NVIDIA data center products and adversely affect revenue.
Dependence on overseas partners, especially in Taiwan and South Korea, poses supply risk if new restrictions impact delivery of components, parts or services.

Demand for AI accelerators is uncertain and depends on the extent and pace of customer adoption of generative AI; customers may face constraints such as insufficient data center capacity or energy, affecting AMD’s revenue.

Climate-related disruptions can delay manufacturing or shipping and drive additional costs; data centers’ dependence on clean water and reliable energy means power or water shortages could impair customers’ expansion and AMD’s product consumption.
Rapid product transitions and industry-wide feature/performance shifts can pressure pricing; delays in customer platform launches or ineffective marketing can cause AMD to miss demand cycles.
Competitive dynamics include NVIDIA’s dominance in the GPU market, which may limit AMD’s ability to compete effectively.
